name: Blackish Plumbeous
lede: Blackish Plumbeous is a very dark bluish grey from Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature, built from *plumbeous*, Latin for leaden, with *blackish* marking how far down the scale it sits.

sections.title: A leaden grey, darkened
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) lists Blackish Plumbeous on plate LII, hue 49′′′′′, tone k, one of several modifier names built on *plumbeous* (lead-colored) [1]. The ISCC-NBS system carried it into its 1955 lists as block 192, *dark bluish gray* [1]. Ridgway's modifier words (*pale*, *light*, *dark*, *blackish*) step a base hue down a tonal ladder rather than naming a new color outright, and the books consulted do not explain why lead, rather than any other grey material, became the reference point [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[pale-charcoal]], [[slate-color]] and [[blue-violet-black]], at 3.1, 3.3 and 3.5 ΔE [1]. It is also close to [[charcoal|Charcoal]], about 6.3 units off, a warmer, slightly darker grey with no blue lean [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 485 of 23,781 paintings, 2.04 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 210, more common than 72 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Paul Sérusier is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 4 of the 26 [[painter:paul-serusier|Sérusier]] paintings in the archive, 5.4 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from [3].

Usage peaks in the 1900s, with 46 of 1,674 paintings from that decade carrying it, 2.6 times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often sits in shadow (35 percent of its 210 within-painting matches), which fits a dark neutral grey [3]. The earliest match dates to 1099, more than eight centuries before the name's 1912 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
